To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the systemic lupus erythematous (SLE) autoantigen calreticulin is released during inflammation, can bind to the globular heads of C1q, can interfere with C1‐mediated immune responses and may therefore contribute to disease pathogenesis.
CRT, a protein released from cells during infection/inflammation, can bind to C1q in a manner that reduces C1q‐binding to immune complexes and to neutrophil surfaces.
calreticulin can bind to C1q, interfere with C1‐dependent immune complex clearance, and is an autoantigenic target in patients with systemic lupus erythematous.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the CRT in the pathogenesis of SLE.
the role of CRT as an autoantibody target, as a regulator of C1q function, and in the pathogenesis of SLE.
the role of CRT as an autoantibody target, as an inhibitor of C1q binding to immune complexes, and its potential as an inhibitor of the classical pathway of complement.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CRT is an autoantigen that may be involved in the development of lupus, but may also have a role in the regulation of the immune response.
CRT is a novel autoantigen that may interfere with complement‐mediated inflammatory reactions.
the CRT‐C1q complex may be involved in the pathogenesis of SLE, and may be a target for future therapeutic intervention.
